en: The inspection (waiting-time) paradox is a classical result of renewal theory, treated for example in William Feller's An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, volume 2. The "friendship paradox" (Scott Feld, 1991, American Journal of Sociology 96(6)), where your friends have more friends than you do, is the same sampling bias. This page is this project's simplified implementation and does not reproduce numbers from any paper.

Bus gaps are 3,000 draws from a gamma distribution (mean = average gap, coefficient of variation = the slider) laid end to end to form the time axis, and passengers are drawn uniformly over the whole axis. The gap a passenger lands in and the time to the next bus are found by binary search. Each point in graph ③ is a run with 3,000 passengers, done 3 times. Class sizes are drawn from the same distribution, rounded to integers and set to at least 1.

You can verify with node tools/validate-inspection.js. The theory is the gap seen = average gap × (1 + CV²) and the average wait is half of that. At irregularity 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2, the measured average waits were 5.0, 5.3, 6.3, 10.1, 16.1 and 25.0 minutes (theory 5.0, 5.3, 6.3, 10.0, 16.3 and 25.0).
The code is available on GitHub.
Regression to the Mean · Simulatio Lab
Even when words have no effect at all, the best performers do worse next time and the worst do better. Run regression to the mean yourself.

People often report that praising a great performance was followed by a worse one, while scolding a bad performance was followed by a better one. It is easy to conclude that "scolding works". Here the true effect of praise and scolding is set to 0. Watch whether the same experience still appears when the words do nothing.

Each person has a fixed skill and a luck draw that is new on every trial. Scores average 50, and a slider sets how much of the spread is luck. At 50% luck, trial 1 and trial 2 scores correlate at 0.5.
After trial 1, the top few percent are praised and the bottom few percent are scolded. Everyone else hears nothing.

Trial 2 keeps the same skill and draws new luck. With the true effect slider at 0, neither praise nor scolding changes any score. Otherwise a + effect is added for the praised and a − effect for the scolded.

The "Sports illustration" scene moves the same calculation to seasons. The top group is on the magazine cover, the bottom group had its worst season, and the true effect applies only to the cover. No real player or magazine data is used.

① Trial 1 and Trial 2 Scores

The horizontal axis is the trial 1 score, the vertical axis the trial 2 score. The dashed diagonal means "exactly the same score next time". Green is the praised (top of trial 1), red the scolded (bottom of trial 1). The blue regression line is flatter than the diagonal, pulling the right end down and the left end up.
The praised (top in trial 1)
The scolded (bottom in trial 1)
Regression line
② Average Change of the Praised and the Scolded

How many points each group changed on average in the next trial. The gold dashed line is the change the words really caused, which sits at 0 when the true effect is 0. The gap between a bar and its dashed line is all regression.
③ The Conclusion the Coach Draws

The coach (or reporter) only sees the difference between the two groups' changes. The black needle is the difference the coach sees, the gold diamond the true difference. Even when the words do nothing, the needle points to "scolding works", and it does not swing back easily as the true effect grows.
④ Depending on the Luck Share

The horizontal axis is the luck share, the vertical axis the average change of each group. With no luck there is no change; the more luck, the more the praised fall and the scolded rise. Dots are three runs with the same settings.
The praised
The scolded

What it shows: Averaging 400 repeats with 50% luck, 400 people, the top and bottom 20% and a true effect of 0, the praised dropped by 7.0 points on average and the scolded rose by 7.1 (theory: ∓7.0). The difference the coach sees was +14.1 points, and in all 400 samples the scolded rose more. The slope of the regression line was 0.50, equal to the reliability (1 − luck share), which is the correlation between the two trials. At 0% luck the change was 0, at 10% it was ∓1.4, at 90% ∓12.6 and at 100% ∓14.0. Picking only the top and bottom 5% gave a change of about ∓10.4, and picking 50% each cut it to about ∓4.0. Even with only 20 people, 97% of samples led to the same conclusion. Praise would have to truly add 7 points and scolding truly subtract 7 (at 50% luck and 20%) before the difference the coach sees reaches 0. In the sports illustration, even with a true cover effect of 0 the cover group changed by −7.0 and the worst-season group by +7.1, and when the cover truly caused −3 points the cover group fell by 10.0, so true effect and regression could not be told apart by eye.

What it doesn't show: This does not mean praise has no effect or that scolding is better. The model sets the true effect to 0, and what real praise and scolding do must be judged with experiments that include a comparison group. The flight instructor story is an anecdote told by Daniel Kahneman in Thinking, Fast and Slow; this page's model is a simplified retelling of it, not an experimental result. The sports scene is likewise only an illustration of the familiar stories "slump after winning rookie of the year" and "slump after a magazine cover". It uses no real player or magazine records and says nothing about whether such jinxes actually exist. The model also assumes skill never changes and luck is independent on each trial, while real skill changes with practice and age.

In Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), Daniel Kahneman explains an anecdote in which a flight instructor came to believe that "praise is followed by worse performance, scolding by better" as regression to the mean. This project's implementation is a simplified model of that anecdote and does not reproduce the anecdote or any figures from the book. The concept of regression itself is generally traced to the work of Francis Galton.
